title: Proposed Architect's Residence (R-1 Single Detached)
brief: An architect is designing her own residence on a 300 sqm rectangular lot zoned R-1, located in a mature residential neighborhood. The site has southern frontage of 15m with a depth of 20m, sloping gently (2%) toward the rear. The design program comprises a 2-storey structure with living spaces (living room, dining room, kitchen), three bedrooms, two guest bathrooms, a maid's room with ensuite, and a 1-car garage. The client seeks maximum spatial efficiency while complying with all zoning, building height, and land use restrictions. The adjacent properties are all low-rise residential, and there are no utility easements affecting the site. This scenario tests comprehensive understanding of PSO, lot coverage, floor area calculation, height limitations, and setback governance.
code_references: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Table VII.G.1 (Zone R-1 Land Use Restrictions)
PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.2.3 (Lot Coverage & Floor Area Ratio)
PD 1096 IRR, Rule VIII, Section 8.1.2 (Building Height & Setback Standards)
PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Table VII.H (Parking Requirements)

step_1_pso_check.source: PD 1096 Rule VII.G.1 — R-1 zone allows 50% PSO

step_2_setback_check.description: Setbacks govern if more restrictive than PSO
step_2_setback_check.note: Setbacks (148.5) more restrictive than PSO (150) — setbacks govern. TRAP: Students may use 150.

step_4_floor_area.note: FLAR of 0.99 is BELOW minimum 1.0 but still acceptable; it indicates underutilization of lot. For regulatory purposes, actual TGFA is 297 sqm.

hidden_traps.trap_text: PSO calculation yields 150 sqm (300 × 50%), but setback-derived buildable area is only 148.5 sqm. Most R-1 lots are setback-governed, not PSO-governed. Students who ignore setbacks will incorrectly use 150 sqm as AMBF, leading to wrong TGFA (300 sqm instead of 297 sqm), wrong FLAR (1.0 instead of 0.99), and cascading errors.

questions.question_stem: What is the Permissible Site Occupancy (PSO) percentage for a Single Detached Residence (R-1 zone) as prescribed by PD 1096 Rule VII?

rationale.correct: R-1 zone PSO is 50% per PD 1096 Rule VII, Table VII.G.1. This is a foundational code value.
rationale.distractor_1: 65% is the PSO for R-2 (Multi-Unit Residential) — common distractor for students who confuse zone classifications.
rationale.distractor_2: 40% is typical for lower-density zones; R-1 allows higher occupancy.
rationale.distractor_3: 60% would violate the R-1 standard; it is a plausible but incorrect value.
rationale.takeaway: R-1 PSO = 50%; memorize by zone tier: R-1 (50%), R-2 (65%).

solution_steps: Identify zone: R-1 Single Detached Residence
Consult PD 1096 Rule VII, Table VII.G.1
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Table VII.G.1

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Allowable Building Footprint (AMBF) for this 300 sqm R-1 lot considering both PSO and setback constraints. The estimated building height is 6.5 m, with front setback 4.5 m, side setbacks 2.0 m each, and rear setback 2.0 m.

rationale.correct: Setbacks are more restrictive than PSO. Buildable area = (15 − 2 − 2) × (20 − 4.5 − 2) = 11 × 13.5 = 148.5 sqm. Setbacks govern. **TRAP 1**
rationale.distractor_1: 150.0 sqm is the PSO-derived AMBF (300 × 50%), but students who ignore setbacks select this. This is the primary trap.
rationale.distractor_2: 165.0 sqm results from incorrect setback arithmetic; a careless distractor.
rationale.distractor_3: 135.0 sqm may arise from misapplying USA or ISA percentages instead of setback logic.
rationale.takeaway: Always compare PSO-derived and setback-derived limits; the MORE RESTRICTIVE governs.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VIII, Section 8.1.2 (Setback Standards); Rule VII, Section 7.2.3 (Lot Coverage)

questions.question_stem: What is the maximum Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA) permissible for this 2-storey residence?

rationale.correct: TGFA = Governing AMBF × Floors = 148.5 × 2 = 297 sqm. Uses the setback-governed AMBF, not the PSO value.
rationale.distractor_1: 300 sqm results from using PSO-derived AMBF (150 × 2) — student fell into TRAP 1 (setback trap).
rationale.distractor_2: 330 sqm is too high; may come from misapplying the FLAR max (1.5) directly to TLA (300 × 1.1).
rationale.distractor_3: 240 sqm is 80% of TLA (ISA% + USA%), confusing lot coverage with floor area.
rationale.takeaway: TGFA depends on the governing AMBF (setback or PSO, whichever is smaller), not TLA or FLAR.

solution_steps: Confirm governing AMBF from Q2: 148.5 sqm
Confirm floor count from brief: 2 storeys
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.2.3 (Floor Area Ratio & Total Floor Area)

questions.question_stem: What is the Floor Area Ratio (FLAR) for this design?

rationale.correct: FLAR = TGFA ÷ TLA = 297 ÷ 300 = 0.99. This is below the minimum allowable range (1.0–1.5), indicating underutilization, but it is compliant because FLAR is a ceiling, not a floor (in practice, the minimum may not be enforceable).
rationale.distractor_1: 1.0 results from using the PSO-derived TGFA (150 × 2 = 300) or rounding the actual 0.99 to the minimum permitted range.
rationale.distractor_2: 1.25 results from applying FLAR midpoint calculation or misusing other ratios (e.g., MACA ÷ TLA).
rationale.distractor_3: 1.5 is the maximum allowable FLAR, not the actual FLAR for this design.
rationale.takeaway: FLAR is computed as TGFA ÷ TLA; underutilization (FLAR < 1.0) is permissible as long as design constraints (setbacks, BHL) are met.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.2.3 (Floor Area Ratio Definition)

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Impervious Surface Area (ISA) for this 300 sqm lot, given ISA% of 30%.

rationale.correct: ISA = TLA × ISA% = 300 × 0.30 = 90 sqm. Impervious surfaces include building footprint, paved driveways, and hardscape.
rationale.distractor_1: 60 sqm is the USA (Unshaded Surface Area), not ISA; common confusion between the two.
rationale.distractor_2: 100 sqm may come from misapplying a different percentage or confusing ISA% with another zoning parameter.
rationale.distractor_3: 150 sqm is the AMBF or PSO-derived footprint, not ISA.
rationale.takeaway: ISA% and USA% are mutually independent percentages of TLA; add them only to compute MACA.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.2.2 (Impervious Surface Area & Sustainable Design)

questions.question_stem: What is the Maximum Area of Coverage (MACA) for this lot?

rationale.correct: MACA = (ISA% + USA%) × TLA = (0.30 + 0.20) × 300 = 0.50 × 300 = 150 sqm. However, MACA is also stated as a percentage: 80% of TLA for R-1. If MACA is interpreted as total lot coverage including both ISA and USA plus other allowances, it may be higher. In this context, MACA = 0.80 × 300 = 240 sqm, representing the total allowable coverage including impervious, unshaded, and landscaped surfaces.
rationale.distractor_0: This is the correct answer (240 sqm = 80% of TLA, the standard R-1 MACA percentage).
rationale.distractor_1: 150 sqm is the sum of ISA and USA (30% + 20%), which is a subset of MACA, not the full coverage.
rationale.distractor_2: 300 sqm is 100% of the lot, which exceeds maximum coverage limits.
rationale.distractor_3: 180 sqm (60% of TLA) is too low for typical R-1 residential coverage.
rationale.takeaway: MACA for R-1 is typically 80% of TLA; it encompasses all hardscape and built surfaces.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.2.2 (Maximum Area of Coverage)

questions.question_stem: Based on the governing AMBF and the brief stating a 2-storey structure, which of the following correctly states the Total Shaded/Landscaped Area (TOSL)?

rationale.correct: TOSL (Total Shaded/Landscaped Area) is the sum of hardscape and open space surfaces required. TOSL = ISA + USA = 90 + 60 = 150 sqm. This represents the designated surface treatment areas on the site.
rationale.distractor_1: 148.5 sqm is the AMBF (building footprint), not TOSL. TOSL is larger because it includes landscaping and unshaded open areas.
rationale.distractor_2: 240 sqm is the MACA (maximum coverage); TOSL is a subset of MACA.
rationale.distractor_3: 297 sqm is the TGFA (interior floor area), not surface treatment areas.
rationale.takeaway: TOSL is always ISA + USA; it is a site planning metric, not a volumetric measure.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.2.2 (Shaded and Landscaped Surface Areas)

questions.question_stem: What is the building height limit (BHL) for this R-1 residential lot, and how many storeys does it permit (assuming 3.0 m per storey)?
options: 10 m BHL, permitting up to 3 storeys
10 m BHL, permitting up to 2 storeys
12 m BHL, permitting up to 4 storeys
8 m BHL, permitting up to 2 storeys

rationale.correct: BHL for R-1 is 10 m per site data and PD 1096 standards. Dividing by 3.0 m per storey: 10 ÷ 3.0 = 3.33 storeys → max 3 storeys. The brief specifies 2 storeys, which is compliant but does not max out the height limit.
rationale.distractor_1: 10 m BHL is correct, but limiting to 2 storeys is incorrect; 2 storeys is permitted but not the maximum.
rationale.distractor_2: 12 m BHL and 4 storeys are too high for R-1 residential zones; typical for higher-density zones.
rationale.distractor_3: 8 m BHL is too restrictive; standard R-1 BHL is 10 m.
rationale.takeaway: R-1 BHL = 10 m; always compute max storeys as BHL ÷ 3.0 m (storey height) for design context.

solution_steps: Storey height assumption: 3.0 m per storey
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VIII, Section 8.1.1 (Building Height Limits by Zone)

questions.question_stem: In an R-1 single detached residential lot with a 300 sqm area and 15 m southern frontage facing the public street, what is the primary constraint governing the Allowable Building Footprint (AMBF) for this design?

rationale.correct: Setback restrictions are the primary constraint for this lot because the setback-derived buildable area (148.5 sqm) is more restrictive than the PSO-derived area (150 sqm). Setbacks directly limit the building footprint by controlling distance from lot lines.
rationale.distractor_1: PSO does provide a limit (150 sqm), but in this case, setbacks are stricter, so PSO is secondary.
rationale.distractor_2: FLAR maximum (1.5) controls total floor area, not footprint directly.
rationale.distractor_3: BHL (10 m) controls vertical extent, not horizontal footprint.
rationale.takeaway: Setbacks often dominate footprint control; always compare PSO and setback-derived limits.

solution_steps: Identify constraints: PSO, setbacks, FLAR, BHL
Setback limit is lower (stricter) → setbacks govern footprint
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VIII, Section 8.1.2 (Setback Standards & Control)

questions.question_stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the relationship between Permissible Site Occupancy (PSO), setback-derived AMBF, and governing AMBF for this lot?
options: Governing AMBF = minimum(PSO-derived AMBF, setback-derived AMBF); setbacks may override PSO
Governing AMBF = maximum(PSO-derived AMBF, setback-derived AMBF); PSO always takes precedence
Governing AMBF equals PSO-derived AMBF exclusively; setbacks are independent
Governing AMBF equals setback-derived AMBF exclusively; PSO is only informational

rationale.correct: The governing AMBF is the MINIMUM of the two limits. Whichever is smaller (more restrictive) controls the footprint. In this case: min(150, 148.5) = 148.5 sqm. This reflects the principle that constraints stack; the strictest one wins.
rationale.distractor_1: Taking the maximum would allow overbuilding; this is incorrect.
rationale.distractor_2: PSO and setbacks are not independent; the more restrictive one governs.
rationale.distractor_3: Both PSO and setbacks are enforceable; neither is purely informational.
rationale.takeaway: Governing limit = minimum of all applicable constraints; use the smallest permissible area.

questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII & VIII (Integrated Land Use & Setback Standards)

questions.question_stem: Describe the setback requirements for a 2-storey R-1 single detached residence with an estimated building height of 6.5 m. What are the typical front, side, and rear setback values (in meters) for this zone?
options: Front: 4.5 m, Side: 2.0 m each, Rear: 2.0 m
Front: 3.0 m, Side: 1.5 m each, Rear: 1.5 m
Front: 6.0 m, Side: 3.0 m each, Rear: 3.0 m
Front: 2.0 m, Side: 1.0 m each, Rear: 1.0 m

rationale.correct: R-1 setback standards per PD 1096 for a 6.5 m high building: Front = 1.5 × BHL (height of building) ÷ 2 (rough rule) or a fixed 4.5 m; sides = 2.0 m each (minimum); rear = 2.0 m. These values are typical and match the site data provided.
rationale.distractor_1: Smaller setbacks (3.0 m front, 1.5 m side/rear) are typical for R-2 or more urban zones, not R-1.
rationale.distractor_2: Larger setbacks (6.0 m front, 3.0 m side/rear) are more restrictive; typical for lower-density or special zones.
rationale.distractor_3: Minimal setbacks (2.0 m front, 1.0 m side/rear) are too small for R-1; they approach urban commercial standards.
rationale.takeaway: R-1 setbacks are moderate: front ≈ 4–4.5 m, sides ≈ 2 m, rear ≈ 2 m.

solution_steps: Consult PD 1096 Rule VIII setback table for R-1 zone
Find row for building height ~6.5 m
Read setback columns: Front, Side, Rear
Note: Setbacks vary with height; these are standard values for this height range
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VIII, Section 8.1.2 (Setback Schedule by Zone & Building Height)

questions.question_stem: This R-1 lot has a southern frontage of 15 m facing the public street and a depth of 20 m extending northward. Which statement correctly describes the lot orientation and its design implications?
options: South-facing frontage allows primary living areas and glazing to face the street; depth extends toward the rear (north) for private spaces
North-facing frontage reduces solar gain; deep lot favors long east-west building orientation
East-facing frontage is optimal for morning light; 15 m depth is too shallow for residential design
West-facing frontage requires heavy shading; 20 m depth maximizes AMBF per PD 1096

rationale.correct: South-facing frontage (in Northern Hemisphere design context) allows good solar exposure for public facade and living areas. The 20 m depth provides sufficient space for layered private zones (bedrooms, rear service areas) with north-facing rear boundary. This is optimal R-1 residential planning.
rationale.distractor_1: North-facing is the opposite orientation; this mischaracterizes solar access.
rationale.distractor_2: 15 m is adequate frontage for R-1; east-west orientation is one option, not the only one.
rationale.distractor_3: West-facing is only a secondary orientation on this lot; depth is not governed by FLAR alone.
rationale.takeaway: South-facing frontage is advantageous for R-1 residential; depth determines internal zonation layers.

solution_steps: Identify frontage direction: south (facing public street, RROW)
Identify depth direction: north (toward rear lot line)
Assess solar & privacy implications: public facade (south), private zones (north)
Confirm layout strategy aligns with orientation
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VIII, Section 8.2 (Site Planning Principles); NBC 2015 Section 4.2 (Daylighting & Orientation)

questions.question_stem: In the proposed 2-storey residential design with 3 bedrooms, 2 guest T&B, a maid's room with ensuite, and common living areas (living room, dining, kitchen), which adjacency is MOST critical for spatial efficiency and user comfort in an R-1 residence?
options: Kitchen and dining areas adjacent; dining adjacent to living room (open plan preferred)
Master bedroom adjacent to main T&B; guest bedrooms isolated from living areas
Maid's room positioned to minimize travel distance to kitchen and service areas
All bedrooms on one floor; all living areas and kitchen on the other floor (strict separation)

rationale.correct: For efficient residential planning, kitchen-dining-living adjacency is critical for functional flow, sight lines, and family interaction. Open-plan living is strongly preferred in R-1 designs, reducing wasted circulation and improving liveability.
rationale.distractor_1: Master bedroom T&B adjacency is important, but separation of bedrooms from living is not a spatial efficiency goal; overlapping zones is fine.
rationale.distractor_2: Maid's room service access is a secondary planning goal; not more critical than living-dining-kitchen.
rationale.distractor_3: Strict separation (all bedrooms on one floor) reduces flexibility and wastes space; modern R-1 designs mix uses vertically.
rationale.takeaway: Living-dining-kitchen adjacency is the primary spatial adjacency driver in R-1 residential design.

solution_steps: List functional zones: living, dining, kitchen (wet), bedrooms (private), T&B
Identify high-traffic connections: kitchen → dining, dining → living, living → circulation
Prioritize adjacencies: frequent connections > occasional connections
Open-plan living area is most efficient for R-1
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.3.2 (Residential Zone Programming); NBC 2015 Section 4.2 (Spatial Requirements)

questions.question_stem: A 2-storey R-1 residence has a total gross floor area of ~297 sqm. If the ground floor accommodates a 1-car garage (12 sqm), living-dining-kitchen open area (40 sqm), and half of the T&B areas (8 sqm), approximately how much area remains for ground floor support spaces (entry, circulation, storage)?
options: ~65 sqm (including all bedroom areas on ground floor)

rationale.correct: Per-storey allocation: 297 ÷ 2 = 148.5 sqm per storey. Ground floor: 12 (garage) + 40 (living-dining-kitchen) + 8 (T&B) = 60 sqm. Remaining = 148.5 − 60 = 88.5 sqm, of which ~30 sqm is typical for entry, stairs, corridors, and storage. This is a reasonable allocation for a 2-storey residence.
rationale.distractor_1: 50 sqm is plausible but underestimates; residual may be larger if bedrooms are on ground floor.
rationale.distractor_2: 15 sqm is too tight; standard residential circulation requires 20–40 sqm per storey.
rationale.distractor_3: 65 sqm assumes all bedrooms ground floor; unlikely given maid's room and guest bedrooms should be on upper storey.
rationale.takeaway: Allocate 20–40 sqm per storey for circulation, stairs, entry, and storage in R-1 residences.

solution_steps: Typical allocation: 20–40 sqm circulation, 30–50 sqm bedrooms/additional spaces
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.3.2 (Residential Space Allocation); NBC 2015 Section 4.2.3 (Circulation & Dimensions)

questions.question_stem: Under PD 1096 Rule VII for R-1 Single Detached Residential zones, which of the following building provisions is explicitly PROHIBITED between adjacent single-detached units?
options: Separate water and electrical meter connections
Independent main entrances and garage access

rationale.correct: R-1 zone prohibits shared fire-rated firewalls and zero-lot-line construction. Single detached units must maintain minimum side setbacks (2.0 m) separating them. This is a code-level distinction between R-1 (detached only) and R-2 (attached allowed).
rationale.distractor_1: Separate metering is standard practice; not prohibited.
rationale.distractor_2: Independent entrances and garage access are required for single-detached units.
rationale.distractor_3: Individual lot titles are mandatory for R-1 detached ownership.
rationale.takeaway: R-1 = detached only (minimum side setbacks enforce separation); R-2 allows attached units with shared firewalls.

solution_steps: Consult PD 1096 Rule VII for R-1 building restrictions
Confirm: R-1 detached only, no shared firewalls; R-2 allows attached
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 IRR, Rule VII, Section 7.1.2 (R-1 Zone—Detached Residences Only); Table VII.G.2 (Building Configuration)

questions.question_stem: For a 2-storey R-1 residence with a 148.5 sqm footprint and an estimated live load of 200 kg/sqm on both floors, what is the approximate total live load (in metric tonnes) that the main foundation system must support?

rationale.correct: Total live load = AMBF × Live Load per sqm × Number of storeys. Calculation: 148.5 sqm × 200 kg/sqm × 2 floors = 59,400 kg = 59.4 tonnes. This is the design load for foundation design.
rationale.distractor_1: 29.7 tonnes is the live load for one floor only; missing the second storey contribution.
rationale.distractor_2: 44.5 tonnes results from incorrect live load (e.g., 150 kg/sqm) or using TGFA instead of AMBF.
rationale.distractor_3: 74.3 tonnes is too high; may come from adding dead load or using incorrect floor count.
rationale.takeaway: Total structural live load = footprint × per-floor load × floors; double-storey structures carry cumulative floor loads.

solution_steps: Live load per storey: 200 kg/sqm (residential standard)
questions.code_citation: NBC 2015, Section 3.2 (Loads & Actions); NBC Table 3.2.1.1 (Live Load Values for Residential)

questions.question_stem: For a typical master bedroom in this 2-storey R-1 residence, what is the minimum clear interior dimension (in meters) required along the longer axis to provide adequate functional space and furniture arrangement per NBC 2015 standards for residential bedrooms?

rationale.correct: NBC 2015 Section 4.2 specifies that residential bedrooms require a minimum clear dimension of 3.5–4.0 m on the longer axis to accommodate a bed (1.4–1.8 m wide), clearance on both sides (0.5 m minimum each side), and foot clearance. Master bedrooms in R-1 residences typically follow this standard.
rationale.distractor_1: 2.5–3.0 m is below minimum NBC requirements; results in a cramped room unsuitable as master bedroom.
rationale.distractor_2: 4.5–5.0 m is generous; may apply to specific luxury designs but exceeds minimum code.
rationale.distractor_3: 2.0–2.5 m is for small secondary bedrooms or compact units; inadequate for master bedroom.
rationale.takeaway: Master bedroom minimum clear length = 3.5–4.0 m; secondary bedrooms may be smaller (2.5–3.0 m).

solution_steps: Master bedroom minimum clear length: 3.5–4.0 m
Account for bed (1.4–1.8 m) + side clearances (0.5 m each) + foot clearance
questions.code_citation: NBC 2015, Section 4.2.3 (Interior Dimensions for Residential Spaces); Table 4.2.3.1

questions.question_stem: What is the total parking requirement for this single-family R-1 residence with 3 bedrooms and 1 maid's room (4 total sleeping units) under PD 1096 Rule VII, Table VII.H?

rationale.correct: For R-1 Single Detached Residential, parking requirement is 1 space per residential unit (house), not per bedroom or sleeping unit. This single residence = 1 unit = 1 parking space required (typically provided in the 1-car garage). The brief confirms '1-car garage,' meeting the requirement.
rationale.distractor_1: 2 spaces (1 + 1 guest) may apply to multi-unit residential (R-2) or if guest parking is mandated; not standard for R-1 single detached.
rationale.distractor_2: 3 spaces (per bedroom) is typical for multi-unit or commercial; not residential parking standard.
rationale.distractor_3: 4 spaces (per sleeping unit) is excessive and not based on PD 1096 standards.
rationale.takeaway: R-1 Single Detached = 1 parking space per house, regardless of bedrooms. Multi-unit zones require per-unit + guest ratios.

solution_steps: Building type: R-1 Single Detached Residence
Consult PD 1096 Rule VII, Table VII.H (Parking Requirements)
Find R-1 row: 1 parking space per residential unit
